clue.text: Evian’s my unfinished still drink

indicators.note: something left unfinished is missing its final part, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: Evian is a French spa town, so its word for 'my' (plural) is the French mes
still and calm are synonyms

explanation.surface: Someone orders a bottle of still Evian water and leaves it half drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Evian looks like the drink; it only tells you to read 'my' in French. Mescal is the Mexican spirit distilled from agave.
explanation.definitionFit: Mescal is a strong Mexican spirit made from agave, so it is one kind of alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Pull in flash new label

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a flash is an instant, and a mo is a moment
to tow is to pull
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A record company pulls in business with a flashy new brand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' reads as an adjective meaning showy; here it is a noun, an instant. The pulling word goes inside the moment, then N follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Motown is the famous Detroit record company, so a music business that releases recordings under its brand name.

clue.text: When farmer’s van drops off pales to support e.g. cattle enclosures

indicators.note: whatever drops off falls away and is lost from the word
in a down clue the supporting part sits underneath, so it comes second

blocks.note: cattle are an example of livestock, called stock
the van, or front, of farmer is its first letter
to pale is to grow faint, to fade

explanation.surface: A farmer's van sheds its load of fence pales by the cattle pens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pales' looks like fence stakes, fitting the enclosures, but it is a verb meaning grows faint. 'Van' means the front, so only the first letter of farmer leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockades are fenced compounds built of upright stakes, used to hold animals or prisoners.

clue.text: One third of GPs avoiding ambitious pain relief

indicators.note: to avoid something is to leave it out, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: GPs has three letters, and the first of them is one third
someone ambitious is aspiring to rise

explanation.surface: A third of family doctors won't prescribe trendy painkillers to patients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One third of GPs' looks like a statistic about doctors; it is just one of the three letters of GPs.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirin is the familiar over-the-counter analgesic tablet taken for headaches and aches.

clue.text: Trespasses over railings, receiving fine

indicators.note: a receiver takes something in, so one part goes inside another

blocks.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
F stands for fine, as on pencil leads
railings are fences

explanation.surface: Someone climbs over the railings to trespass and is fined.
explanation.walkthrough: Over and railings join into one string, and the fine letter is taken in just after the cricket O.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespasses in the old sense are sins or wrongdoings, as in the Lord's Prayer, so misdeeds or crimes.

clue.text: Police careful in court after gangsters discharged

indicators.note: a thing discharged is unloaded and emptied, so only its shell remains
one part following another comes later in the line

blocks.note: fly in British slang means sharp, knowing, wary
taken as written
the word emptied of its middle
a quad is a quadrangle, a college courtyard

explanation.surface: The police take care in court after some gangsters are acquitted.
explanation.walkthrough: The Flying Squad is the Metropolitan Police unit that tackles armed robbery; 'discharged' suggests released defendants but means emptied of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Flying Squad is a specialist London detective unit, so a branch of the police force.

clue.text: English politician starts to rant over rubbish outside the back of Caffè Nero?

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters
the back of a word is its final letter
here 'outside' just means placed beyond, sitting on the far side of the next part

blocks.note: E abbreviates English
an MP is a Member of Parliament
its last letter
the first letters of three words

explanation.surface: An English MP rants about the litter dumped outside a branch of the coffee chain Caffè Nero.
explanation.walkthrough: Caffè Nero is a British coffee-shop chain, so the coffee name hides the definition: Nero was a Roman ruler. The initials follow the coffee's final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero ruled Rome as its fifth emperor, so he is an example of an imperial monarch, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Very distressed in revolutionary set with Corfu’s extremists

indicators.note: extremists are those at the extremes, the two ends of a word
a revolution turns things right round

blocks.note: the end letters of Corfu
to set something down is to put it

explanation.surface: A tourist is upset to find a band of revolutionaries on Corfu, the Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' is a verb, not a group; 'revolutionary' turns it round, and Corfu's end letters go in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To be cut up is an informal British idiom for being deeply upset or grief-stricken.

clue.text: Somewhere in Lancashire street, glass broken by man

indicators.note: a thing broken into is split open, so something else is pushed into the gap

blocks.note: St is the standard abbreviation for street
a man is referred to as he
a lens is a shaped piece of glass, as in spectacles

explanation.surface: On a Lancashire street, a man smashes a window pane.
explanation.walkthrough: Street and glass sit side by side, and the pronoun for a man splits them. St Helens is a town in Merseyside, historically Lancashire, famous for Pilkington glass.
explanation.definitionFit: St Helens is a town historically within the county of Lancashire in north-west England, so it is one place there.

clue.text: Former party leader who’s associated with a hammer and sharp sickle, ultimately?

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the final letters are taken

blocks.note: Thor, the Norse thunder god, wields a hammer
the last letters of the two words

explanation.surface: The hammer and sickle conjure up a communist party boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The hammer and sickle point to a communist, but the leader is Jeremy Thorpe, head of the British Liberal Party from 1967 to 1976.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeremy Thorpe led the UK Liberal Party, so he is a past head of a political organisation.

clue.text: Injury cover is cheap, yet complicated

indicators.note: something complicated is twisted and tangled, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An insurance policy for injuries is cheap but full of complex small print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Injury cover' sounds like insurance; it is a literal cover worn over a hurt eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A patch worn over a damaged or injured eye literally covers the wound while it heals.

clue.text: Fire rifle at home? It’s a bloomer

blocks.note: to fire someone up is to rouse or wake them
to rifle a house is to ransack and rob it
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Firing a gun indoors would be a blunder, a bloomer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like British slang for a blunder; it is a flowering plant. 'Fire' and 'rifle' both pretend to be about guns.
explanation.definitionFit: Wake-robin is a common name for wild flowering plants such as cuckoo-pint and trillium, so it blooms.

clue.text: In which dish is out, presumably?

definitions.text: In which dish is out, presumably?

blocks.clueFragment: In which dish is out, presumably?
blocks.note: surface reading: a meal where a dish has been taken off the menu
setter's reading: a 'dish' is a very attractive person, and 'out' means unconscious, so a good-looking person deeply asleep

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' and 'out' suggest serving food, but a dish is slang for a looker and out means asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the extra rest supposed to keep a person looking attractive, so a lovely person dozing is presumably taking it.

clue.text: Spin round parking and drive back

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one part wraps another

blocks.note: to reel is to whirl or spin
P is the road-sign symbol for parking

explanation.surface: A driver spins the car round in a car park and reverses out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive back' reads like reversing a car; it means fend off an attacker.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel an enemy is to force them to retreat, pushing an attack away.

clue.text: Operative checking trap’s set?

blocks.note: surface reading: a secret agent or worker making sure a snare is primed
setter's reading: trap is slang for the mouth, and a set is a set of teeth, examined by someone who operates

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' suggests a snare and 'set' suggests ready to spring; in slang the trap is the mouth, and its set is the teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dentist who performs operations examines patients' teeth, so this professional checks the set in your mouth.

clue.text: Source of fancy Met logo seen around Yard unknown

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamental, so the letters are dressed up in a new order
a thing seen around another encircles it

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
Y abbreviates yard
algebra uses x, y and z for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: The designer of the Metropolitan Police's flashy new logo, seen around Scotland Yard, is anonymous.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met and the Yard both point to London's police, whose headquarters is Scotland Yard; here Yard is only its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Etymology traces where a word comes from, so it is the origin or derivation of that word.

clue.text: I can be seen in river area following one liqueur

indicators.note: whatever is seen within something sits inside it
one part following another comes after it in the line

blocks.note: taken as written
the Tamar is the river dividing Devon from Cornwall
the Roman numeral for one
A abbreviates area

explanation.surface: Someone says they can be found by the river, sipping a liqueur.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tamar is the river forming most of the border between Devon and Cornwall in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Tia Maria is a sweet Jamaican coffee-flavoured spirit, a branded after-dinner drink.

clue.text: Hornist possibly hard to find

definitions.note: a cryptic reading: the printed word is what the phrase describes, not a synonym of it

blocks.note: first meaning, read in reverse: the seven letters of 'in short', put into a supple, bendy order, spell this word
second meaning: scarce, with demand outstripping stock

explanation.surface: Horn players, perhaps, are rare to come by.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the phrase, read as an instruction, makes the printed word. 'In short' supplies the letters and 'supply' as an adverb, suppl-y or pliably, says shuffle them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scarce, with demand outstripping stock, is difficult to obtain or locate.

clue.text: Eccentric old bishop drinking Double Diamonds – every one!

indicators.note: one who drinks takes something inside

blocks.note: O abbreviates old
the first letter of Diamonds, written twice because of Double
B is the chess notation for bishop
every one is all

explanation.surface: A strange old bishop downs every bottle of Double Diamond, a British pale ale.
explanation.walkthrough: Double Diamond was a well-known British beer, but here it is two Ds for diamonds. They sit inside old plus bishop, and ALL closes the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddball is an informal noun for a peculiar, unconventional person, the same as an eccentric.

clue.text: In good form, become tired, swapped at the front for Hazard

indicators.note: swapping the fronts of two words exchanges their opening sounds

blocks.note: someone in good form is fit
to pall is to grow tiresome or weary

explanation.surface: Eden Hazard, the footballer, was in good form but tired and got substituted.
explanation.walkthrough: Hazard was a star Belgian forward at Chelsea, so 'swapped' sounds like a substitution. The two words trade their first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitfall is a hidden danger or trap, so a risk or peril waiting to catch someone out.

clue.text: There’s cycling book …

indicators.note: letters going round a cycle move from the front to the back

blocks.note: the word with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone points out a book about cycling, continued in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the sentence on into 22, but this clue stands alone: the last two letters ride round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is a book of the Old Testament, telling of the Jewish queen of Persia.

clue.text: Used gestures to indicate setter’s in the sea

indicators.note: a thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the setter is 'I', and setter's is I'm, I am
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A swimmer waves to signal that the setter is out in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter's is read as 'setter is', so I'M, which goes inside the Med.
explanation.definitionFit: To mime is to act something out with movements and no words, communicating by gesture.

clue.text: … on the counter, its dimensions somewhat thick

indicators.note: somewhat means to a partial degree, so only some of the letters are used
counter means against the direction, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Continuing 20: the book on the shop counter is rather thick for its size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' suggests a shop counter; it means reading backwards. 'Thick' is a noun here, as in the thick of the fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The thick of something is its centre, where activity is most intense, the same as its middle.

clue.text: Dissident publication curtailed in South America

indicators.note: to curtail is to cut short, so the tail letter is lost
a thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: S abbreviates south
an edition is one publication of a work
the US is America

explanation.surface: An underground newspaper in South America is censored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South America' looks like one place but splits into S and US, with the shortened publication between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe opposing established authority and stirring up rebellion against the state.

clue.text: Hot-looking drink the German overturned

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end

blocks.note: decaf is decaffeinated coffee
der is the German masculine 'the'

explanation.surface: A German knocks over his drink, which must have been hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot-looking' suggests a hot drink, but it means flushed. The whole string flips, not each part separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a flushed face from heat, embarrassment or exertion appears overheated.

clue.text: Large adult about to squeeze into my protective boot

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way
squeezing into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
A is the film certificate for adult
both are exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: A big grown-up struggles to squeeze into a pair of protective boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation, as in 'My, how you've grown', not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A galosh is a waterproof rubber overshoe worn to keep ordinary footwear dry.

clue.text: Maybe Springbok striking head is unable to run off

indicators.note: striking out the head removes the opening letter

blocks.note: is unable becomes can't
to elope is to run off secretly to marry

explanation.surface: A South African rugby player, a Springbok, is concussed by a blow to the head and cannot run.
explanation.walkthrough: The Springboks are South Africa's rugby team, so the clue reads as a sporting injury; the springbok is also a gazelle.
explanation.definitionFit: The springbok is a southern African gazelle, one example of the hoofed grazing animals of that family.

clue.text: Song boring a musician

indicators.note: boring drills into something, so one part goes inside

blocks.note: a lay is a ballad or song
a, as in 'a pound a day', means per

explanation.surface: A song strikes a musician as dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like dull, but it means drilling into. 'A' as in 'ten pence a go' becomes the Latin per.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is someone who plays an instrument, such as a guitar or piano player.
